strengths: The core motivation is well-articulated and convincing: scaling video length is temporal extrapolation rather than interpolation (Fig. 1), and the paper clearly identifies the fidelity–horizon tension between scarce long-video supervision and abundant short-video priors.

The method is technically coherent: decoupling the mean-seeking SFT flow-matching objective (long-range coherence) from the mode-seeking reverse-KL/DMD teacher alignment (local realism) via a shared encoder and two lightweight heads (DDT) is a sensible way to resolve the described gradient interference, and it naturally yields a few-step sampler at inference.

The ablation study (Table 2) directly tests the three key claims: dual-head decoupling, sliding-window DMD, and SFT anchor, and the largest drop when removing the dual heads supports the gradient-interference motivation.

Useful engineering details are provided in the appendix (sequence parallelism, variable-length bucketing, the image-latent boundary mismatch fix for sliding-window DMD following LongLive, data sources and lengths), which improves reproducibility of a non-trivial training recipe.
The paper is honest that its method is orthogonal to causal AR approaches and identifies concrete future directions (Appendix E).
weaknesses: The central claim of 'minute-scale' generation is not supported by the evaluation: all quantitative results are on 30-second videos; no minute-scale results, metrics, or failure analysis are presented.

The 'best overall' claim is overstated by Table 1: Long-context SFT beats the proposed method on subject consistency and VLM consistency (77.28 vs 75.42), and MixSFT is essentially tied on motion smoothness; wins are mainly in dynamic degree, aesthetic, and image quality. The paper acknowledges AR baselines get inflated consistency by being static/over-saturated, but the same scrutiny is not applied to its own numbers, and no variance/statistical significance is reported.

The NFE comparison conflates two effects: the proposed method is a 4-NFE distilled model, while the strongest SFT baselines run at 50 NFE. Since DMD distillation is known to boost perceptual sharpness, it is unclear how much of the local-quality gain comes from the decoupling idea versus simply distilling a few-step sampler; a 50-NFE version of the model or a distilled SFT baseline would disentangle this.

Novelty is largely compositional: DDT dual heads (Wang et al., 2025c), DMD/VSD reverse-KL distillation (Yin et al., 2024), and sliding-window teacher alignment (CausVid/APT2-line work) are all established; the contribution is their combination for long video, and the paper itself notes the DM-head-only long generation resembles APT2.

The 'No SFT' ablation is theoretically puzzling: the text asserts the short teacher is 'strictly blind' to long-context structure, yet the DM head is never trained with long-video supervision beyond the shared encoder, so how it achieves 0.9579 consistency is not explained.

Evaluation is narrow: a single 200-prompt prompt set, VBench-derived automatic metrics plus one MLLM (Gemini) judge; no human evaluation, no temporal flickering despite citing it, and aesthetic-quality values in the 0.5–0.7 range lack calibration/context. Stronger long-video baselines from the cited related work (Self-Forcing++, SkyReels-V2, test-time-training methods) are discussed but not compared.

Key training hyperparameters (λseg, steps, learning rates, rollout sampling strategy for on-policy windows) are not specified in the main text, and no code/model release is stated, limiting reproducibility.

Presentation has notable blemishes: the duplicated contribution sentence in the introduction, inconsistent baseline naming (LongSFT/MixSFT vs Long-context SFT/Mixed-length SFT), and Eq. (9)'s notation (introducing v_ψ^(k) after use) makes the core surrogate hard to follow.

strengths: The core motivation is clear and well-articulated: the observation that extending temporal horizon is 'extrapolation' rather than 'interpolation' (Fig. 1), and that scarce long-video data induces a fidelity–horizon tradeoff, is a plausible and underexplored framing.

The proposed method is technically coherent: decoupling the mean-seeking SFT flow-matching objective from the mode-seeking reverse-KL (DMD/VSD) teacher alignment via separate heads on a shared encoder is a sensible resolution of the stated gradient-interference problem, and the sliding-window DMD implementation details (Supp. Sec. C, handling image/video latent mismatch at window boundaries) show genuine engineering care.

The evaluation covers both SFT-style and AR-distillation baselines, uses an established protocol (VBench-Long) plus an MLLM-based consistency score with an anti-static guard in the prompt, and includes an ablation of the three main components.
The few-step (NFE=4) long-video inference capability is a practical benefit if the claims hold.
weaknesses: A critical missing baseline: the obvious competitor is a two-stage pipeline — SFT on long videos followed by standard few-step DMD distillation — which would test whether the joint decoupled training is actually necessary. The ablation only removes the dual heads (naive single-head joint training), not the sequential alternative, so the central architectural claim is under-supported.

The headline quantitative claims are overstated relative to Table 1. 'Ours' is not best on subject consistency (0.9682 vs. 0.9685), background consistency (0.9548 vs. 0.9614), or motion smoothness (0.9863 vs. 0.9874); margins on the metrics where it does win are small, and 'best overall performing model' relies on a subjective weighting of columns.

Evaluation is thin: 200 prompts, 30-second generations, a single seed, no variance/confidence reporting, and heavy reliance on Gemini-3-Pro for the headline VLM consistency score, a metric susceptible to prompt engineering (the authors control the judging prompt). Distilling Wan 1.3B into a Wan 1.3B student and evaluating with VBench risks circularity between teacher and student priors.

Key implementation details needed for reproducibility are absent from the main paper: λ_seg, learning rates, training iterations, number of rollout steps, window overlap strategy during training, and compute budget. Supp. Sec. A/B covers only GPUs, sequence parallelism, and coarse dataset statistics (100k videos, avg. 31s).

The claim that the DM head — trained only on sliding-window reverse-KL — can 'directly generate long videos end-to-end bidirectionally' is surprising and under-analyzed. The mechanism (long-range information reaching the DM head only through the shared encoder, which itself is trained on window-cropped DMD gradients of student rollouts) deserves direct evidence or analysis; the paper cites APT2 but offers no measurement of how much long-range coherence the DM head actually carries versus the FM head.

The ablation (Table 2) uses only three metrics with small differences (e.g., consistency 0.9615 vs. 0.9604 for removing sliding-window DMD), making it hard to distinguish real effects from noise, and it omits the human evaluation or user study that qualitative fidelity claims of this kind typically require.

Novelty is modest: each ingredient (DMD/VSD reverse-KL distillation, sliding-window teacher alignment, DDT dual heads, mean-seeking vs. mode-seeking framing) exists in prior work; the contribution is primarily their combination, which would be acceptable if the empirical case for the combination were stronger, but the missing sequential baseline and thin evaluation undermine this.

The central conceptual argument (Fig. 1: mixed-duration training causes 'softer, less alive' outputs because long-horizon training is extrapolation) is asserted rather than directly tested — e.g., no window-level fidelity measurement isolating where MixSFT loses sharpness relative to the teacher.

strengths: The core observation (Fig. 1) that temporal length extrapolation for videos is fundamentally different from spatial resolution interpolation is compelling and well-articulated, providing a clear motivation for decoupling local fidelity from long-range coherence.

The method is technically coherent: combining a DDT-style shared encoder with separate FM (mean-seeking SFT) and DM (mode-seeking reverse-KL via DMD/VSD) heads is a sensible resolution of the gradient-interference problem, and the sliding-window reverse-KL formulation (Eq. 5) is cleanly stated.

The few-step inference capability (NFE=4) via the DM head is a practical advantage over 50-NFE SFT baselines, and Table 1 shows the method is best overall on a mix of quality, motion, and consistency metrics.

The ablation study (Table 2) directly tests the central claim: removing the dual-head design causes the largest degradation, supporting the gradient-interference motivation rather than just the overall recipe.

The supplementary detail on handling image-latent vs. video-latent mismatch at sliding-window boundaries (App. C) is a non-obvious implementation insight that will be useful to practitioners; the Gemini evaluation prompt (App. D) that penalizes 'trivially consistent' static videos is a thoughtful evaluation choice.

The method requires no additional short-video data beyond teacher velocity queries, which is a meaningful practical claim, and the limitations/future work discussion (App. E) is honest, e.g., regarding orthogonality to causal AR methods.
weaknesses: The central 'minute-scale video' claim is not fully supported by the evaluation: quantitative comparisons (Table 1) evaluate only 30-second generation, and training data is capped at 61 seconds. The abstract and conclusion repeatedly claim minute-scale synthesis, but no experiment demonstrates true minute-scale outputs, creating a claim-evidence gap.

No variance or statistical reporting: differences in Table 1 and Table 2 are often small (e.g., subject consistency 0.9615 vs. 0.9604 for 'No Sliding-window DMD', motion smoothness 0.9863 vs. 0.9874 for Mixed-length SFT), yet no error bars, number of seeds, or significance analysis is provided. Some ablation deltas may be within metric noise.

The baseline set is somewhat weak or mismatched: LongSFT/MixSFT are 50-NFE SFT baselines while CausVid/Self-Forcing/InfinityRoPE are 4-NFE AR methods evaluated via extrapolation, so the comparison conflates sampling budget and paradigm. Stronger recent long-video baselines (e.g., Self-Forcing++, LongLive, Blockvid, test-time-training approaches) are cited but not compared.

The evaluation relies on 200 prompts and VBench-Long-style metrics that the authors themselves acknowledge can be gamed (consistency metrics reward static/over-saturated outputs), plus a single Gemini-3-Pro score; a human evaluation is absent, which is a notable gap for a paper whose claims center on subjective local sharpness and 'aliveness'.

Reproducibility is only partially addressed: key hyperparameters (lambda_seg, fake-score update cadence, total training compute, resolution) are not specified in the main text, and no code release is stated; only a supplemental website with videos is mentioned.

Presentation issues: the contribution bullet list sentence is duplicated ('We summarize our key contributions as follows' appears twice in consecutive paragraphs), and the Impact Statement is boilerplate with no discussion of deepfake/misuse concerns relevant to a long-video generator.

The claimed benefit of inheriting 'high-fidelity short-timescale priors' is supported mainly by indirect metrics (aesthetic/image quality); no direct measurement of local fidelity relative to the teacher (e.g., teacher-vs-student window quality) is provided.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the paper argues convincingly that extending video generation from seconds to minutes is temporal extrapolation rather than interpolation (Fig. 1), and identifies a real fidelity–horizon trade-off when training on mixed-duration data.

The core design is sensible: routing mean-seeking (flow matching SFT on long videos) and mode-seeking (reverse-KL DMD/VSD alignment to a short-video teacher on sliding windows) objectives into separate lightweight decoder heads over a shared encoder is a clean resolution of the stated gradient-conflict problem, and the ablation (Tab. 2) shows the naive single-head combination performs worst.
Practical end-to-end payoff: using only the DM head at inference yields few-step (NFE=4) minute-scale generation without a separate distillation stage, which is a tangible systems contribution.

Reasonably broad empirical evaluation: comparisons against SFT baselines (Long-context, Mixed-length) and rollout/AR baselines (CausVid, Self-Forcing, InfinityRoPE, LongLive) across VBench-Long-style metrics, a 60-second stress test, and a 31-participant user study; the user study consistently favors the method at both horizons.

Honest limitations discussion: the paper acknowledges failure modes in compositional temporal instructions and event-level planning, and clearly flags that the 60-second table is a stress test, not a complete benchmark.
weaknesses: The headline claim that the method 'effectively closes the fidelity–horizon gap' is only partially supported by the evidence. In Tab. 1, the simple Long-context SFT baseline actually matches or slightly beats the proposed method on subject consistency (0.9685 vs 0.9682), motion smoothness (0.9866 vs 0.9863), and VLM consistency (77.28 vs 75.42). The clear wins are on dynamic degree, aesthetic/image quality, and human ratings—so the paper improves the sharpness/dynamics axis but does not demonstrably close the consistency axis, contradicting the abstract's framing.

Novelty is incremental: each ingredient (rectified flow SFT, DMD/VSD reverse-KL distillation, DDT dual heads, sliding-window teacher alignment, the LongLive image-latent re-encoding trick for window boundaries) is established prior work; the contribution is their composition. The related-work positioning is fair, but reviewers should not over-credit the decomposition as a fundamentally new technique.

The strong claim that mixed-length training is 'fundamentally flawed' is asserted more than demonstrated. In Tab. 1, Mixed-length SFT is actually second-best on several metrics (e.g., image quality 0.6683, background consistency 0.9541), which softens the paper's own motivating argument.

Evaluation scope is limited: 200 test prompts, 30-second generations as the primary benchmark, and the 60-second stress test omits the SFT baselines entirely (because they would need retraining), making the one-minute evidence asymmetric and harder to interpret. The ablation table (Tab. 2) reports only three opaque aggregated metrics without stating exactly how 'Consistency/Motion/Quality' are computed.

Reproducibility gaps: the internet-scraped video subset is described only as 'randomly collected internet videos' with filtering criteria unspecified; key hyperparameters (λseg weighting, fake-score update schedule details, rollout/window sampling frequencies) are not given in the main text, and no code release is stated. The mixture includes a private data source, limiting exact replication.

The 'expert short-video teacher' is the same Wan 2.1 1.3B model used as the student's base, which makes the teacher-distillation narrative somewhat circular: the student is largely recovering the base model's own local prior after long-video SFT degrades it, rather than transferring capability from a genuinely stronger/expert teacher. This weakens the generality of the paradigm's claims.

Data ethics treatment is thin: training on scraped internet video (including 'randomly collected' sources) raises copyright/consent questions that the boilerplate impact statement does not address; the related-work section also reads as citation-stuffed, diluting the genuinely relevant prior work.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem — the fidelity–horizon gap when scaling video generation from seconds to minutes — and articulates the motivation (temporal extrapolation is not analogous to resolution interpolation, Fig. 1) clearly and persuasively.

The decoupled dual-head design (mean-seeking FM head on long videos + mode-seeking DMD head on sliding windows over a shared encoder) is a sensible resolution of the gradient-interference conflict, and the motivation in Sec. 3.3 is well argued.

The ablation study (Tab. 2) directly tests the central claims: removing the dual heads causes the largest drop, confirming the gradient-interference hypothesis; removing SFT or DMD each degrades complementary aspects.

Evaluation is multi-modal: automatic VBench-Long metrics (Tab. 1), a 60-second stress test (Tab. 3), a user study with 31 participants (Tab. 4), and qualitative comparisons. The method leads on dynamic degree and quality metrics while remaining competitive on consistency, and the user study results are consistent with the automatic metrics.

The limitations section is honest and specific (failure on compositional temporal instructions, revisitation, event-level planning), and the paper clearly flags that the 60-second table is a stress test rather than a complete benchmark.

Practical engineering details (sliding-window DMD with image-latent boundary handling, DeepSpeed Ulysses, variable-length bucketing) make the recipe concretely reproducible in spirit, and the few-step (NFE=4) inference is a tangible benefit.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty. The method is a recombination of existing components: DDT (Wang et al., 2026b) for head decoupling, DMD/VSD (Yin et al., 2024b;a) for the reverse-KL surrogate, and the LongLive boundary re-encoding trick for sliding-window DMD. The core insight — route mean-seeking and mode-seeking signals to disjoint heads — is intuitive but incremental.

A theoretical gap that is not addressed: Eq. (5) matches only sliding-window marginals q^(k) to the teacher, which places no constraint on the joint distribution across windows or on transitions between windows. The paper asserts this yields long-range coherence, but coherence is entirely inherited from the shared-encoder SFT; there is no analysis of why marginal window matching does not introduce inconsistency at window boundaries, nor of the mode-collapse risk inherent to reverse KL. No diversity or FVD metric is reported to check for mode collapse.

The quantitative gains are mixed and modest. In Tab. 1, 'Ours' is not best on subject consistency (0.9682 vs. CausVid 0.9736), background consistency, or aesthetic quality (0.5735 vs. 0.6044); the strongest wins are on dynamic degree, which the authors themselves note baselines trade off deliberately. No statistical significance, confidence intervals, or per-prompt variance is reported across the 200-prompt test set.

The inference-time claim that the DM head 'can directly generate long videos end-to-end bidirectionally' despite being supervised only on sliding windows rests on the shared-encoder argument and is only empirically supported, not mechanistically explained. It is unclear whether this would hold at other scales or with a weaker teacher.

Reproducibility gaps: λseg, learning rates, training iterations, and total compute (A100/GB200 hours) are not reported; data curation ('filter out single-shot videos from randomly collected internet videos') is under-specified, with no discussion of licensing or provenance beyond a boilerplate impact statement.

The framing that a short-video teacher 'absorbed web-scale diversity' is weakened by the experimental setup where the teacher is the same Wan 1.3B model as the student — the teacher is not actually an independent expert in the reported quantitative comparisons.

Baseline comparisons mix NFE regimes (50 vs. 4), and the 60-second evaluation excludes retrained SFT baselines; while the paper is upfront about this, it means the headline minute-scale claim is only partially validated.
The ablation table reports only three aggregate metrics with no details on which setting the ablations were run in (model scale, horizon, prompt set), limiting their interpretability.

strengths: The core idea is well motivated and clearly articulated: decoupling local fidelity (mode-seeking sliding-window reverse-KL alignment to a frozen short-video teacher) from long-term coherence (mean-seeking SFT flow matching on scarce long videos) is a sensible decomposition, and the observation that video length extrapolation differs from image resolution interpolation is a useful framing.

The method is technically grounded in established tools (DDT-style dual heads, DMD/VSD gradients), and the engineering solutions—e.g., re-encoding the decoded RGB prefix as an image latent to resolve the image/video latent mismatch at sliding-window boundaries—are non-trivial and practically valuable details.

The evaluation is reasonably comprehensive: automatic metrics on a 30-second benchmark (Tab. 1), a 60-second stress test (Tab. 3), a user study with 31 participants (Tab. 4), and an ablation (Tab. 2) that isolates each of the three claimed ingredients. The ablation supports the central gradient-interference argument: removing the dual-head design produces the largest degradation.

The paper is honest about metric caveats (e.g., noting that rollout-based methods can be over-saturated or static, which inflates consistency metrics) and the Gemini evaluation prompt explicitly penalizes trivially-static videos, which strengthens the credibility of the VLM consistency metric.
Limitations are discussed substantively, including concrete failure cases (compositional temporal instructions, revisitation vs. genuinely cyclic routes), rather than boilerplate.
weaknesses: Some quantitative claims are overstated relative to the numbers. In Table 1, Long-context SFT achieves a higher VLM consistency than the proposed method (77.28 vs. 75.42), and several other metrics are effectively tied (e.g., subject consistency 0.9685 vs. 0.9682), yet the text claims the method 'stands out as the best overall performing model.' The 'best overall' framing should be more carefully hedged or supported by significance analysis.

No statistical uncertainty is reported anywhere: no error bars or variance across prompts/seeds in Tables 1–3, and several margins in the ablation are small (e.g., consistency 0.9615 vs. 0.9604 for 'No Sliding-window DMD'). It is unclear whether the differences are meaningful.

Reproducibility is limited. Key hyperparameters are missing: the value of λ_seg, the form of the DMD weighting λ(t), learning rates, training iterations, batch sizes, number of DMD surrogate updates, and the 200-prompt test set composition are not specified. The test prompts appear to be self-constructed rather than a public benchmark subset, which hinders independent comparison.

The user study (Tab. 4) is under-specified: the rating scale, interface, and instructions are not described, no inter-rater reliability or significance tests are reported, and only 31 participants rate a modest number of sets.

Baselines are not perfectly matched: the 60-second stress test excludes SFT-only baselines (acknowledged), and LongLive's NFE is 'not directly comparable.' The claim of orthogonality to causal AR methods is plausible but untested experimentally.

The central claim that mixed-duration training is 'fundamentally flawed' is more of an argument-by-analogy (Fig. 1) than a rigorous analysis; the experimental evidence is consistent with a fidelity-horizon trade-off but does not establish the strong 'extrapolation vs. interpolation' thesis conclusively.
Data provenance is thin: 'randomly collected internet videos' are used without discussion of licensing or consent, and the impact statement is perfunctory for a generative video model.
